In the narrow belly of St. Jude’s Lane, between a cooperage that smelled of wet cedar and a baker who only worked at night, Arthur kept a shop for mending shadows.

He did not advertise. There was no painted shingle swinging above the lintel, only a small pane of smoked glass set into the oak door. Those who needed Arthur always found him, guided less by street numbers than by an obscure, dragging heaviness in the small of their backs.

Most people went their entire lives assuming a shadow was a passive consequence of sunlight—a flat, obedient mimic pinned to the heels. They did not realize that a shadow is a second skin, woven from memory, consequence, and gravity. Like any garment worn daily against the abrasive surface of the world, it could fray. It could snag on an unkept promise, tear along the seam of a sudden grief, or grow dangerously thin where a person had spent too many years pretending to be smaller than they were.

Arthur was seventy-two, with fingers stained the gray of old slate and eyes that had grown slightly milky from decades of peering into dim corners. His workshop smelled of cold tallow, dried lavender, and the faint, ozone tang that rises off river stones after a lightning strike.

On a Tuesday when the autumn air was turning the color of bruised plums, the brass bell above the door gave a thin, metallic chime. 

A young woman stood on the threshold. She wore a tailored wool coat, buttoned to the chin, and her hair was pinned back with severe, practical efficiency. To a casual observer on the street, she would have looked immaculate—a picture of tidy, functioning adulthood.

Arthur, however, looked down.

Her shadow was a disaster.

It did not trail cleanly behind her. Instead, it pooled around her boots like spilled ink, tangled and ragged, bunched into dense, fibrous knots. Worse, along its western edge, it was frayed into long, weeping ribbons that dragged along the floorboards like wet lace. It looked three times heavier than she was.

"Come in, child," Arthur said, laying down his bone-handled awl. "Close the latch. The draft makes the edges curl."

She stepped inside, her movements stiff, as if she were carrying an invisible sack of grain on her shoulders. "A friend told me," she began, her voice tight, dry. "She said you fixed things. Silly things."

"Nothing about the dark is silly," Arthur said mildly. "Step onto the lime slab, please."

In the center of the room lay a square of pale limestone, illuminated by a single skylight overhead. She climbed onto it with a quiet sigh of effort. As she did, her shadow spread across the white stone, and Arthur could see the full extent of the damage.

He knelt, his old knees cracking like dry twigs. He took a pair of horn-rimmed spectacles from his pocket and leaned close.

"Ah," he murmured, lightly brushing his fingertips over the stone. To her, it would feel like a cold breeze across the ankles. "An echo-snag. A bad one."

"It hurts to walk," she whispered, her tidy posture beginning to crack. "Not my legs. Just... moving forward. Every step feels like walking through deep mud. I wake up exhausted."

"That’s because you’re dragging someone else’s weight," Arthur said softly. 

He pointed to the tangled mass near the silhouette of her ribcage. There, woven inextricably into the silhouette of her own body, was the faint, phantom outline of a second set of broad shoulders, an extra hand reaching outward, a distinct jawline that did not belong to her.

"When someone leaves," Arthur explained, not looking up, "we are supposed to let the shared fabric part naturally. It leaves a raw hem, yes. It stings for a season. But people are clumsy. They panic at the tearing sound. They take needles of guilt and fear, and they whipstitch the other person’s ghost into their own silhouette, thinking it will keep them whole."

A single tear tracked through the powder on her cheek, though her face remained otherwise still. "If I let it go, there’s nothing left of him."

"There is the memory of him," Arthur said gently. "Memory belongs in the mind, where it can rest. The shadow belongs to the body. If you force the body to carry what only the heart is built to hold, you will eventually cease to move at all."

She closed her eyes. The shop was quiet, save for the ticking of an old regulator clock on the wall and the distant rattle of an iron-wheeled cart on the cobblestones outside.

"Fix it," she breathed. "Please."

Arthur reached into his waist-pouch. He did not use steel needles or thread made of cotton. For this work, he drew out an obsidian blade no larger than a willow leaf, and a spool of twine spun from the fibers of twilight—gray, supple, and entirely weightless.

"Hold very still," he warned. "It will feel cold. Like stepping into a pond in November."

He set to work. With the delicate precision of a surgeon, Arthur slipped the obsidian blade between the threads of her shadow and the foreign dark that clung to it. 

With every severed stitch, the room seemed to exhale. A faint, low hum—the sound of long-trapped silence escaping—filled the air. The dark ribbons began to loosen. Where the phantom shoulders had been grafted, Arthur made three clean, decisive cuts, unhooking the phantom grip from her heels.

The foreign shadow did not vanish; instead, without her weight to anchor it, it softened, turned to a light, harmless ash of gray, and drifted slowly toward the floorboards, dissolving into the quiet dust of the shop.

Then, Arthur took his twilight thread. With swift, looping motions of his fingers, he bound up her frayed edges. He smoothed the silhouette of her hips, tucked in the loose fibers along her spine, and anchored the hem firmly back to the soles of her shoes. 

"There," he said, sitting back on his heels with a soft grunt. "Step down."

She opened her eyes and blinked. Slowly, tentatively, she took a step off the limestone slab.

She gasped. 

It was subtle, but Arthur saw it: her chin rose an inch. The tension in her collarbones vanished. She took a second step, then a third, walking across the shop floor with a light, springing grace she had likely forgotten she possessed. 

Behind her, her shadow followed—sleek, clean-edged, and entirely hers. It moved when she moved; it paused when she paused. It was dark, yes, because life under the sun is full of substance, but it was no longer heavy.

"What do I owe you?" she asked, reaching for her purse, her hands trembling slightly.

"Nothing that jingles," Arthur said, standing up and brushing the stone dust from his aproned knees. "Just leave the door open a crack when you walk out. The shop needs the light."

She looked at him for a long moment, a profound, unnamable gratitude in her eyes, then nodded. 

When she opened the oak door, the late afternoon sun broke through the clouds, spilling a broad swath of gold across the threshold. She stepped into it, and for the first time in a very long time, she cast only one shadow into the world.

Arthur watched her go. Then he picked up his broom, swept the gray dust into a neat little pile in the corner, and sat back down by the window to wait for the next heavy soul to find the lane.
